Bail and the Egmore Magistrate courts

  1. Home
  2. /
  3. Practice areas
  4. /
  5. Criminal Law
  6. /
  7. Bail Lawyer Egmore

Legal framework and scope

A bail lawyer advises on and represents people who have been arrested or are in custody, so that they can apply to be released while the case is pending. Shasti Law Firm acts in bail matters. Consultations are by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. The firm has no office at Egmore, and nothing on this page says that it appears before any particular court.

Egmore is one of the main locations of the Chennai Metropolitan Magistrate courts. The official Chennai court list shows a Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court, an Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court, a number of Metropolitan Magistrate courts and several special courts there, and the Allikulam Complex is listed separately for some of them. The Egmore Courts Guide sets out the listing.

For the general explanation of regular and anticipatory bail, see Regular Bail Lawyer in Chennai and Anticipatory Bail Advocate in Chennai. This page is about how bail connects with the Egmore courts.

Which code applies?Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the CrPC, IPC and Indian Evidence Act for new proceedings. Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

Bail at the Magistrate stage

After an arrest the person must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours, not counting travel time (Article 22(2) of the Constitution). The Magistrate considers remand and, within the powers the law gives, can consider bail. For many offences a Magistrate can grant bail. For others, generally the more serious ones, the application is made to the Court of Session or the High Court. Which applies depends on the offence and the stage, and is explained at the consultation.

Regular bail, default bail and anticipatory bail

Regular bail

Sought by a person who has been arrested, so that they are released while the case is pending. The court considers factors such as the nature and seriousness of the accusation, the person’s antecedents, any risk of absconding or tampering with evidence, and the conditions that can be imposed.

Default (statutory) bail

Where the investigation is not completed within the time the law allows, the accused may have a right to bail on that ground (Section 187(2) BNSS, earlier Section 167(2) CrPC). The period depends on the offence.

Anticipatory bail

Sought before an arrest, and heard by the Court of Session or the High Court and not by a Magistrate, even at Egmore. See anticipatory bail.

The special courts listed at Egmore

The official list includes special courts at Egmore, such as courts for Economic Offences Wing cases, a Mahila Court and a Commercial Court. A case is assigned to such a court because of the nature of the case and the allotment orders, and not because of where the parties live. A listing at Egmore does not mean any Egmore court will hear a given matter.

If a family member has been arrested

Time matters, but a hurried step can also cause problems. These are general points.

  • Find out the police station, the crime number and the sections alleged.
  • Ask for a copy of the FIR and the arrest memo.
  • Note when the arrest took place and when the person was produced before a Magistrate.
  • Gather identity and address proofs for the person and for any proposed surety.
  • Contact the office as early as you can for a consultation.

How a consultation works

Consultations are held by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. We note the stage and the next date, review the FIR and remand papers and explain the options and risks. The court for your case is decided by jurisdiction and confirmed from the papers. No outcome can be promised.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • Copy of the FIR and arrest memo
  • Remand application or remand order, if available
  • Identity and address proofs of the accused and of proposed sureties
  • Medical or other records bearing on custody, if relevant
  • Any earlier bail order or case details

General procedure

  1. 1Consultation to confirm the stage, the sections alleged and the next date.
  2. 2Review of the FIR, remand papers and any earlier orders.
  3. 3Identification of the forum: Magistrate, Court of Session or High Court.
  4. 4Drafting and filing of the bail application, with grounds and surety details.
  5. 5Appearance on the dates fixed and compliance with any bail conditions.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Which court hears a bail application at Egmore?
It depends on the offence and the stage. A Magistrate court can consider bail within its powers, and for other offences the application goes to the Court of Session or the High Court. Which Egmore court, if any, hears a case is decided by allotment orders.
Can anticipatory bail be granted by an Egmore Magistrate court?
No. Anticipatory bail is a remedy before the Court of Session or the High Court, and not before a Magistrate.
What is default bail?
Where the investigation is not completed within the period the law allows, the accused may have a right to bail on that ground (Section 187(2) BNSS). The period depends on the offence.
How soon must an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate?
Within 24 hours of arrest, not counting the time needed to travel to the Magistrate (Article 22(2) of the Constitution).
Does the firm have an office at Egmore?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai.
Can bail be guaranteed?
No. Courts decide each application on its facts, and no lawyer can promise bail.

Anticipatory Bail Lawyer in Chengalpattu

Anticipatory bail and the Chengalpattu district

Legal framework and scope

Anticipatory bail is a direction that a person be released on bail if arrested, sought when there is a genuine apprehension of arrest for a non-bailable offence. For proceedings under the new codes it is governed by Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (the successor to Section 438 of the CrPC). Shasti Law Firm prepares such petitions. Consultations are by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. The firm has no office in Chengalpattu.

Chengalpattu is a district of its own, and Tambaram, Alandur and Pallavaram are in it. The district directory lists the Principal District Court and an Additional District Court at the Chengalpattu complex, along with Magistrate courts there. The directory does not describe each court’s separate powers, so which court takes up an application is confirmed from its own records for each case. See the Chengalpattu Courts Guide.

This page is about the Chengalpattu connection. For the general explanation of what courts look at and what documents are useful, see Anticipatory Bail Advocate in Chennai.

Which code applies?Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the CrPC, IPC and Indian Evidence Act for new proceedings. Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

Which court hears anticipatory bail

Both the Court of Session and the High Court can hear an application for anticipatory bail. A Magistrate court does not usually hear one, even where Magistrate courts are listed in the same place.

Whether to approach the Court of Session or the Madras High Court, and which Court of Session, depends on the facts, including where the case is registered and where the offence is alleged to have happened. That decision is made at the consultation from the FIR or complaint.

If the case is from Tambaram, Alandur or Pallavaram

Many people from these areas first look for a court in their own locality. The Tambaram and Alandur complexes are listed with Sub Courts, Munsif courts and Magistrate courts. See the Tambaram Courts Guide and the Alandur Courts Guide. For criminal cases from these areas, see Criminal Lawyer in Tambaram and Criminal Lawyer in Alandur.

What a petition generally sets out

The petition sets out the facts, the nature of the dispute, the applicant’s antecedents and willingness to cooperate with the investigation. Courts typically look at the gravity of the accusation, any risk of absconding or tampering with evidence, and whether the accusation appears to be aimed at causing humiliation. The court may impose conditions, and each application is decided on its facts and in the court’s discretion. No outcome can be promised.

If you have only received a notice

A police notice under Section 35 BNSS (earlier Section 41A CrPC) asks a person to appear. It is not an arrest, and it should not be ignored. If you fear arrest after receiving one, take advice before the date given.

If an arrest has already happened

Anticipatory bail is sought before an arrest. After an arrest, the remedy is regular bail. See Regular Bail Lawyer in Chennai and Bail Lawyer in Egmore.

How a consultation works

Consultations are held by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. We review the FIR or complaint, the notice and your papers, explain which forum may suit and what the petition would involve, and note any dates. The court is decided by jurisdiction and is confirmed for your case.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • Copy of the FIR or complaint, if registered and accessible
  • Any police notice or summons, including a notice under Section 35 BNSS
  • Government photo ID and proof of address
  • Documents bearing on the allegations
  • Details of any earlier cases or orders

General procedure

  1. 1Consultation to understand the allegation and the basis for the apprehension of arrest.
  2. 2Review of the FIR or complaint and a decision on the forum: Court of Session or High Court.
  3. 3Drafting the petition with the facts, antecedents and undertakings.
  4. 4Filing and listing, and appearance on the dates fixed.
  5. 5Compliance with any conditions the court imposes.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Which court grants anticipatory bail for a Chengalpattu district case?
The Court of Session or the Madras High Court. Which of them, and which Court of Session, depends on the facts and is decided from the FIR. A Magistrate court does not usually hear it.
Is there a separate court for anticipatory bail at Tambaram or Alandur?
The directory lists Sub Courts, Munsif courts and Magistrate courts at both complexes. It does not list a Court of Session as such, and it does not describe each court’s powers, so the court is confirmed for each case.
Can I apply for anticipatory bail after being arrested?
No. It is sought before an arrest. After an arrest, the remedy is regular bail.
Does a police notice mean I will be arrested?
Not necessarily. A notice to appear is not an arrest, but it should not be ignored. If you fear arrest, take advice early.
Does the firm have an office in Chengalpattu?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai.
Can anticipatory bail be guaranteed?
No. Courts decide each application on its facts and in their discretion, and no lawyer can promise it.

Legal framework and scope

A criminal lawyer advises and represents people accused of an offence, from the first police notice or summons through the investigation and trial. Shasti Law Firm acts for accused persons. Consultations are by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. The firm has no office at Egmore, and nothing on this page says that it appears before any particular court.

Egmore is one of the main locations of the Chennai Metropolitan Magistrate courts, and the official list shows a larger and more varied set of courts there than elsewhere in the city. People often search for an "Egmore court lawyer" without knowing which of those courts, if any, will hear their case. The Egmore Courts Guide sets out the listing. This page explains how a case reaches a court there.

This page is about the trial side of a criminal case. For bail after arrest, see Bail Lawyer in Egmore. For the wider picture, see Criminal Defence Lawyer in Chennai.

Which code applies?Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the CrPC, IPC and Indian Evidence Act for new proceedings. Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

The courts the official list shows at Egmore

  • The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court and an Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court.
  • Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate courts for Economic Offences Wing cases.
  • A number of numbered Metropolitan Magistrate courts.
  • Fast Track Courts at Magisterial Level and special Metropolitan Magistrate courts listed at the Allikulam Complex, including courts for land-grabbing cases and for fake stamp paper and fake currency cases.
  • A Mahila Court at Egmore and another at the Allikulam Complex, and a Commercial Court.

The list tells you that a court exists. It does not tell you that your case will be heard there.

How a criminal case reaches a court at Egmore

Through the police

After an FIR, the police investigate and, if they find enough material, file a charge sheet before the Magistrate who has jurisdiction. The accused is then summoned or produced. Which Magistrate court that is depends on the offence, where it is alleged to have happened and the orders allotting cases to particular courts.

Through a private complaint

A person can also file a complaint directly before a Magistrate. Complaints of this kind are common in cheque dishonour cases. A summons follows if the court takes the complaint on file.

Through a special court

Cases investigated by a particular agency, or of a particular kind, can be assigned to a special court. That assignment follows the nature of the case and not where the accused lives.

What a summons or charge sheet means for you

A summons fixes a date to appear. Ignoring it can lead the court to issue a warrant, so it should be answered. A charge sheet is the police report of the investigation. Getting certified copies of it and of the witness statements is usually the first step in preparing a defence. See Criminal Defence Lawyer in Chennai for discharge applications and trial defence, and regular bail if an arrest has happened.

Offences that go beyond a Magistrate

More serious offences are tried by a Court of Session, and the case is committed to it by the Magistrate. Anticipatory bail is likewise a Court of Session or High Court remedy. See anticipatory bail and High Court criminal lawyer.

How a consultation works

Consultations are held by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. We read the FIR, complaint, summons or charge sheet with you, note the next date, identify the likely court and stage, and explain the options and risks. No outcome can be promised. The court for your case is decided by jurisdiction and confirmed from the papers.

  • FIR or private complaint, and the charge sheet if filed
  • Statements of witnesses, if already obtained
  • Photo ID and proof of address
  • Documents that bear on the allegation
  • Details of any earlier bail order

  1. 1Consultation to understand the allegation, the court and the next date.
  2. 2Review of the FIR or complaint and, once filed, the charge sheet.
  3. 3Obtaining certified copies and deciding whether to seek discharge or to defend at trial.
  4. 4Appearance on the dates fixed, cross-examination and arguments.
  5. 5Advice on appeal or revision where the law allows.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Which Egmore court will hear my case?
The official list shows many courts at Egmore. Which one, if any, hears a case depends on the offence, the place it is alleged to have happened, the agency involved and allotment orders. It is confirmed from your papers.
Does the firm have an office at Egmore?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai.
What happens if I do not answer a summons?
The court may issue a warrant. Keep the summons, note the date and take advice promptly.
Can an Egmore Magistrate court try every offence?
No. More serious offences are tried by a Court of Session. Which court tries an offence depends on the law and the sections alleged.
Is a special court at Egmore chosen by where I live?
No. Special courts are assigned because of the nature of the case, such as an agency investigation, and not by residence.

Legal framework and scope

A criminal lawyer advises and represents people accused of an offence or named in a criminal complaint. Shasti Law Firm acts for accused persons. Consultations are by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. The firm has no office at Saidapet, and nothing on this page says that it appears before any particular court.

The official Chennai court list shows several numbered Metropolitan Magistrate courts at Saidapet, and a fast-track court at Magisterial Level for cases under the Negotiable Instruments Act. Many people therefore search for a Saidapet criminal lawyer when they receive a cheque dishonour summons. The Saidapet Courts Guide sets out the listing. This page explains how those cases reach a court there, and what a Saidapet listing does not decide.

For family matters at Saidapet, see Family Court Lawyer in Saidapet. For the wider picture, see Criminal Defence Lawyer in Chennai.

Which code applies?Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the CrPC, IPC and Indian Evidence Act for new proceedings. Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

Cheque dishonour complaints and Saidapet

A complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is filed before a Magistrate after a cheque is returned unpaid and a statutory notice has gone unanswered. Where it can be filed turns on the connecting facts the Act provides (Section 142(2)), such as where the payee’s bank branch is, and not on where the accused lives or where the lawyer is. A cheque dishonour case from Saidapet can therefore be heard elsewhere, and a case heard at Saidapet can concern a person from another part of the city.

See Cheque Bounce Advocate in Chennai and Section 138 NI Act for the stages and the notice period.

Other criminal cases before a Saidapet Magistrate

Metropolitan Magistrate courts are criminal courts of first instance. They deal with complaints and police cases for offences triable by a Magistrate, and with matters such as remand and bail within a Magistrate’s powers. Which Saidapet court takes a case is fixed by allotment orders that change from time to time, so this page does not say which police stations fall within which court.

When a case does not stay with the Magistrate

More serious offences are tried by a Court of Session, and anticipatory bail is a Court of Session or High Court remedy and not a Saidapet Magistrate remedy. See anticipatory bail and regular bail.

If you have received a summons or notice

  • Note the court, the case number and the date given.
  • Keep the summons, the complaint and any cheque or bank memo.
  • Do not ignore a summons. The court may issue a warrant if you do not appear.
  • For a cheque notice, note the date you received it, because the reply period runs from it.
  • Take advice before you reply or sign anything.

Clients from Saidapet and nearby areas can request a consultation. Consultations are held by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. We read the complaint or summons with you, identify the stage and the next date, explain the options and the risks, and confirm the court from the papers. No result can be promised.

  • Agreements, invoices or messages behind the transaction
  • Photo ID and proof of address
  • Any earlier reply or court order

  2. 2Review of the complaint, notice and documents, and confirmation of the court.
  3. 3Advice on a reply, settlement possibilities or a defence.

  5. 5Advice on appeal or revision where the law allows.

No. The venue depends on connecting facts such as the payee’s bank branch (Section 142(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act), and not simply on the local area.

Several numbered Metropolitan Magistrate courts and fast-track courts at Magisterial Level, including one for Negotiable Instruments Act cases. The list does not say which police station areas each serves.

No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai.

No. Anticipatory bail is heard by the Court of Session or the High Court.

Legal framework and scope

A family court lawyer advises on and represents people in family disputes: divorce, maintenance, child custody and visitation, and related proceedings. Shasti Law Firm acts in these matters for either spouse. Consultations are by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. The firm has no office in Chengalpattu, and nothing on this page says that it appears before any particular court.

The Chengalpattu district directory lists a Family Court at the Chengalpattu complex, along with a Mahila Court and an Additional Mahila Court. It does not list a Family Court at Tambaram or Alandur. Family Courts are set up under the Family Courts Act, 1984 to deal with matrimonial and family disputes. Whether a petition from a given address belongs to the Chengalpattu Family Court or to another is a question of territorial jurisdiction, and this page does not answer it for you.

For the questions that residents of Tambaram and Alandur most often ask, see Divorce Lawyer in Tambaram and Divorce Lawyer in Alandur. For the general picture, see Family Court Advocate in Chennai.

What the district directory lists

  • A Family Court at the Chengalpattu complex.
  • A Mahila Court and an Additional Mahila Court at Chengalpattu.
  • No Family Court at the Tambaram or Alandur complexes, which are listed with civil and Magistrate courts.

The directory is a list of courts. It does not set out which areas each court serves, so the notified area of the Family Court is confirmed from the court’s records before a petition is filed.

Kinds of family case

Divorce

By mutual consent, where both spouses agree, or contested, where one spouse petitions on a ground the law recognises. See mutual divorce and contested divorce.

Maintenance

Support for a spouse, children or, in some cases, parents, claimed under the law that applies to the parties. See maintenance.

Child custody and visitation

Orders on who a child lives with and how the other parent has contact, decided with the child’s welfare as the main concern. See child custody.

How a family case usually proceeds

A petition is filed and notice goes to the other side. Family Courts often refer the parties to counselling or mediation before evidence begins. Interim applications, for example for maintenance while the case is pending, can be made along the way. The time taken depends on the case and the court, and no result can be promised.

Related matters

A family dispute can include a complaint under the Domestic Violence Act. Those applications go to a Magistrate and not to the Family Court. See Domestic Violence Lawyer in Tambaram and Domestic Violence Lawyer in Chennai.

Shasti Law Firm acts in these matters for either side as the facts require. The firm welcomes consultation enquiries from clients in Pallavaram. If you are in immediate danger, contact the police on 112 first. This page gives general information and is not a substitute for emergency help.

The general explanation of the Act and the kinds of relief is on the Domestic Violence Lawyer in Chennai page, and the Chengalpattu district position is explained on Domestic Violence Lawyer in Tambaram. This page covers what is specific to Pallavaram.

Which court deals with an application from Pallavaram

Applications under the Act go to a Magistrate. The Chengalpattu directory lists a District Munsif cum Judicial Magistrate Court at Pallavaram. It lists no Mahila Court there; it lists Mahila Courts at Chengalpattu and an Additional Mahila Court at Alandur. This page does not say that an application will be heard at any of them.

Section 27 of the Act lets an application be made to the Magistrate within whose local limits the aggrieved person lives or works, or the respondent lives, or the cause of action arose. More than one court may therefore be possible, and which is right is decided from the facts. See the Pallavaram Courts Guide and the Chengalpattu Courts Guide.

If you want to make an application

An application is prepared from the facts and the documents. A consultation covers what has happened, who the respondent is, where each person lives, what relief is needed and what evidence exists. If you have received a notice or application

A notice from the Magistrate fixes a date to appear. Do not ignore it. Keep every paper, note the court and the date, and take advice promptly so that a reply can be prepared in time. Whether the court can hear the application is also a point to check early.

How this differs from divorce

An application under this Act is separate from a divorce petition and from a criminal complaint. Some people need more than one, and they may be heard in different courts. See Divorce Lawyer in Pallavaram.

Magistrate court or Sessions court?

Legal framework and scope

A bail lawyer helps a person who has been arrested, or is in custody on remand, apply to be released while the case is pending. Shasti Law Firm welcomes consultation enquiries from clients in Kanchipuram. Consultations are by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office. The firm has no office in Kanchipuram, and nothing on this page says that it appears before any particular court.

This page is about bail after arrest. If an arrest has not happened but is feared, see Anticipatory Bail Lawyer in Kanchipuram. For the wider criminal process, see Criminal Lawyer in Kanchipuram.

Which code applies?Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the CrPC, IPC and Indian Evidence Act for new proceedings. Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

Which court can grant bail

The district pages list a Chief Judicial Magistrate Court and Judicial Magistrate Courts No. I and No. II at Kancheepuram, a Principal District and Sessions Court, and Magistrate courts at Sriperumbudur and Uthiramerur. A Magistrate can grant bail in many cases. For some serious offences the application must go to the Court of Session or the High Court. The offence, the stage and the court where the person was produced decide it. See the Kanchipuram Courts Guide.

Kinds of bail after arrest

  • Regular bail: sought after arrest, from the court that has the case.
  • Default bail: where the investigation is not completed within the time the law allows, the accused may have a right to bail on that ground (Section 187(2) BNSS).
  • Interim or conditional release: a court may impose conditions such as reporting to a police station.

Surety and conditions

Bail usually needs a surety, and the court may attach conditions. A surety is a person who undertakes that the accused will attend court. Identity and address papers for the surety are normally needed, and the surety’s details are checked by the court. The exact requirements are set by the court that grants bail.

How a consultation works

A family member can attend the appointment at West Mambalam with the remand order, the FIR copy and the case number. We check which court has the case and what has been filed, and set out the options. Whether the firm can take up the application before that court is confirmed at that stage.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • The FIR copy and the remand order
  • The name of the court and the case or crime number
  • Identity and address proof of the accused and of any proposed surety
  • Any earlier bail order or rejection
  • Medical or other papers relevant to custody, if any

General procedure

  1. 1Confirming where the person was produced and which court has the case.
  2. 2Reading the FIR and remand order and checking the stage.
  3. 3Preparing and filing the bail application with the surety papers.
  4. 4Attending the hearing and following the conditions if bail is granted.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Can a Kanchipuram Magistrate always grant bail?
No. A Magistrate can grant bail in many cases, but for some serious offences the application must go to a higher court. This is confirmed from the offence charged.
What is default bail?
Where the investigation is not completed within the time the law allows, the accused may have a right to bail on that ground (Section 187(2) BNSS).
Is a bail application filed at Chengalpattu or at Kancheepuram?
Kancheepuram and Chengalpattu have separate district judiciaries. The court that has the case, which is confirmed from the remand papers, decides where the application is filed.
Does the firm have an office in Kanchipuram?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai.
Can bail be guaranteed?
No. Each application is decided on its facts, and no lawyer can promise bail.

Legal framework and scope

Anticipatory bail is an order that a person who fears arrest on an accusation of a non-bailable offence can seek in advance, so that if arrested they are released on bail. It is dealt with in Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (the successor to Section 438 of the CrPC). Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

Which court hears an anticipatory bail petition

The petition goes to the Court of Session or to the Madras High Court. A Magistrate court does not usually hear it.

The district pages list a Principal District and Sessions Court at Kancheepuram.   • A person who has received a police notice and is worried it may lead to arrest.
  • A person in a family, property or business dispute that has turned into a criminal complaint.

What the court may consider

A court looks at the nature of the accusation, the accused’s background, whether the person is likely to cooperate with the investigation and whether custody is needed. It may impose conditions. The result depends on the facts, and none can be promised.

Bring the FIR or complaint, any notice, and a short account of events. We check where the case is registered, whether a petition can be filed in a Sessions Court or must go to the High Court, and how urgent it is. Whether the firm can take up the petition before that court is confirmed at that stage.

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • The FIR copy, complaint or police notice
  • A dated account of events and the names of the parties
  • Identity and address proof
  • Papers on any related civil, family or business dispute
  • Any earlier bail or anticipatory bail order

Domestic Violence Lawyer in Kanchipuram

Advice for people in Kanchipuram and nearby areas who want to make an application under the Domestic Violence Act, or who have received one.

Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

  1. Home
  2. /
  3. Practice areas
  4. /
  5. Matrimonial & Family Law
  6. /
  7. Domestic Violence Lawyer Kanchipuram

Legal framework and scope

A domestic violence lawyer advises on and represents people in proceedings under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. Shasti Law Firm acts in these matters for either side as the facts require. The firm welcomes consultation enquiries from clients in Kanchipuram. Consultations are by appointment at the West Mambalam, Chennai office, and the firm has no office in Kanchipuram.

If you are in immediate danger, contact the police on 112 first. This page gives general information and is not a substitute for emergency help.

The general explanation of the Act, the kinds of relief and how it differs from divorce and criminal complaints is on the Domestic Violence Lawyer in Chennai page. This page covers what is specific to Kanchipuram: which court an application may go to.

Which court deals with an application from Kanchipuram

Applications under the Act go to a Magistrate. The district pages list a Chief Judicial Magistrate Court and Judicial Magistrate Courts No. I and No. II at Kancheepuram, with Magistrate courts at Sriperumbudur and Uthiramerur. The pages reviewed list no Mahila Court, and this page does not say whether one exists.

Section 27 of the Act lets an application be made to the Magistrate within whose local limits the aggrieved person lives or works, or the respondent lives, or the cause of action arose. More than one court may therefore be possible, and which is right is decided from the facts. See the Kanchipuram Courts Guide.

If you want to make an application

An application is prepared from the facts and the documents. A consultation covers what has happened, who the respondent is, where each person lives, what relief is needed and what evidence exists. The Act provides for several kinds of relief, including protection and monetary relief, and which can be sought depends on the case. No result can be promised.

If you have received a notice or application

A notice from the Magistrate fixes a date to appear. Do not ignore it. Keep every paper, note the court and the date, and take advice promptly so that a reply can be prepared in time. Whether the court can hear the application is also a point to check early.

How this differs from divorce

An application under this Act is separate from a divorce petition and from a criminal complaint. Some people need more than one, and they may be heard in different courts. See Divorce Lawyer in Kanchipuram.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • Details of the relationship and the addresses of both parties
  • Dates and descriptions of the incidents, as far as they can be recalled
  • Medical papers, messages or photographs, if any
  • Any police complaint or earlier order
  • Papers on income and expenses, if monetary relief is needed

General procedure

  1. 1First meeting: what has happened and what help is needed.
  2. 2Checking where each party lives and which court can hear the application.
  3. 3Preparing and filing the application, or the reply to it.
  4. 4Attending the hearings and following the court’s orders.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Which court hears a domestic violence application from Kanchipuram?
A Magistrate. The district pages list Magistrate courts at Kancheepuram, Sriperumbudur and Uthiramerur, and Section 27 allows more than one possible court. The right one is confirmed from the facts.
Is there a Mahila Court at Kanchipuram?
The pages reviewed list none. This page does not say whether one exists.
Do I need a divorce petition as well?
Not necessarily. The Act deals with protection and relief and is separate from a divorce petition.
Does the firm have an office in Kanchipuram?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai.
Can a result be guaranteed?
No. Courts decide each case on its facts, and no lawyer can promise a result.

Criminal Law

Regular Bail and Anticipatory Bail before the Madras High Court

What regular and anticipatory bail mean, which court can hear each, and when a bail matter may be taken to the Madras High Court.

Bail matters before the Madras High Court, Chennai

  1. Home
  2. /
  3. Practice areas
  4. /
  5. Criminal Law
  6. /
  7. High Court Bail Lawyer Chennai

Legal framework and scope

Bail is release from custody, on conditions, while a criminal case is pending. This page is about bail matters that are before, or may reach, the Madras High Court. Its formal name is the High Court of Judicature at Madras, and people also search for it as the Chennai High Court. Shasti Law Firm prepares and argues regular bail and anticipatory bail petitions where the matter is one the High Court can hear. Consultations are by appointment at the firm’s only office, in West Mambalam, Chennai. The firm has no office at the High Court, George Town or Parrys Corner.

For the general explanation of each remedy, see Regular Bail Lawyer in Chennai and Anticipatory Bail Advocate in Chennai. For quashing petitions, revisions and appeals, see High Court Criminal Lawyer in Chennai. No result can be promised in any bail matter.

Which code applies?Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the CrPC, IPC and Indian Evidence Act for new proceedings. Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

Is the High Court the first place to ask for bail?

Not necessarily, and the High Court is not the only forum. Depending on the offence and the stage of the case, a bail application may lie before a Magistrate, before the Court of Session, or before the High Court. The provisions that deal with bail in non-bailable offences and with the special bail powers of the High Court and the Court of Session are in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). Section 483 BNSS is the provision that corresponds to Section 439 of the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure.

The High Court may expect the remedy before the Magistrate or the Court of Session to be considered first, so a direct High Court petition is not always suitable. Which route is right is decided on the facts of each matter and is confirmed at the consultation.

What is the difference between regular bail and anticipatory bail?

  • Regular bail is sought after arrest, by a person who is in custody. The court decides whether to release the person on bail, usually on conditions.
  • Anticipatory bail is sought before arrest, by a person who has a reasonable apprehension of being arrested for a non-bailable offence. It is dealt with in Section 482 BNSS (earlier Section 438 CrPC), and both the Court of Session and the High Court can hear such applications.
  • Anticipatory bail is not a general protection from the law. It operates in relation to a particular accusation, the court can impose conditions, and the person is expected to cooperate with the investigation.

When can a bail matter reach the Madras High Court?

The situations in which a bail matter is commonly taken to the High Court include the following. Whether any of them applies, and whether it is advisable, depends on the order, the reasons and the law.

  • A regular bail or anticipatory bail application has been refused by the Court of Session and a further application to the High Court is considered.
  • The offence or the stage of the case is such that the High Court is the court with the power to hear the bail application.
  • Bail or suspension of sentence is sought while an appeal against conviction is pending. Section 430 BNSS (earlier Section 389 CrPC) deals with this.
  • A bail condition is to be modified, or an order granting bail is challenged or defended.

What does a High Court bail petition usually deal with?

A petition sets out the facts, the allegation and the sections invoked, the period already spent in custody where relevant, the stage of the investigation or trial, and the applicant’s background and willingness to comply with conditions. The court looks at matters such as the seriousness of the allegation, the likelihood of the person absconding or interfering with witnesses, and any special statute involved. Some special laws, such as the NDPS Act, carry their own conditions for bail, and these can change what must be shown.

Which other courts may be involved?

Bail is often first considered by a Metropolitan Magistrate or by a Sessions-level court in Chennai, and the same case may later come to the High Court. George Town and Parrys Corner are older parts of Chennai long associated with the city’s courts. A locality name does not tell you which court hears a matter, so the offence, the stage and the court that holds the case decide the venue. See the George Town and Parrys Courts Guide and the Chennai Courts Guide.

How to request a consultation

Bring the FIR or case number, any order already passed, the dates of arrest or remand, and the names of the courts involved. If time matters, say so when you call, and we will tell you what the next step could be. Whether the firm can take up a particular matter is confirmed at that stage.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • FIR or complaint, and the case or crime number
  • Remand order, arrest memo or notice, if any
  • Earlier bail orders or rejection orders, with their reasons
  • Charge sheet or final report, if filed
  • Identity and address proof, and details of sureties where relevant
  • A dated chronology of events

General procedure

  1. 1Consultation, and review of the FIR, the orders so far and the stage of the case.
  2. 2Deciding the forum: Magistrate, Court of Session or High Court, and whether it is regular or anticipatory bail.
  3. 3Preparing the petition with the supporting documents and any grounds on conditions.
  4. 4Filing, listing and hearing, including any interim direction the court considers.
  5. 5Complying with the conditions of any order, and considering the next remedy if bail is refused.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Can I apply for bail directly in the Madras High Court?
Sometimes, but not always. The law and the High Court’s own practice may expect the Magistrate or the Court of Session to be approached first. This is decided on the facts of the case.
What is the difference between regular bail and anticipatory bail?
Regular bail is sought after arrest. Anticipatory bail is sought before arrest, when a person apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence, and is dealt with in Section 482 BNSS.
What if the Sessions Court has refused bail?
A further application to the High Court may be considered. Whether it is advisable depends on the reasons for the refusal and on any change in circumstances.
Is Section 528 BNSS the same as bail?
No. Section 528 concerns the High Court’s inherent powers, for example to quash proceedings. Bail is a separate remedy.
Does the firm have an office at the Madras High Court?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai, and consultations are by appointment.
Can a bail result be guaranteed?
No. Each court decides on the facts and the law, and no lawyer can promise a result.

Matrimonial & Family Law

Family Court Appeals and Related Proceedings before the Madras High Court

How a decision of a Family Court can be taken to the Madras High Court, what cannot be appealed, and why the time limit matters.

Appeals from the Family Courts to the Madras High Court

  1. Home
  2. /
  3. Practice areas
  4. /
  5. Matrimonial & Family Law
  6. /
  7. Family Court Appeal Lawyer Madras High Court

Legal framework and scope

A family matter is first heard by a Family Court, not by the High Court. This page is about what happens after the Family Court has decided: an appeal, or a related proceeding, before the Madras High Court. The High Court’s formal name is the High Court of Judicature at Madras, and it is also searched for as the Chennai High Court. Shasti Law Firm advises on such appeals. Whether the firm can take up a particular appeal is confirmed at the consultation. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai. It has no office at the High Court, George Town or Parrys Corner.

For work before the Family Court itself, see Family Court Lawyer and Advocate in Chennai. For appeals in divorce cases in particular, see Divorce and Matrimonial Appeal Lawyer. No outcome can be promised.

When can a Family Court decision be appealed to the Madras High Court?

Section 19(1) of the Family Courts Act, 1984 provides that an appeal lies to the High Court from every judgment or order of a Family Court that is not an interlocutory order, on both facts and law. An interlocutory order is an order made along the way, such as one on a procedural step, and is generally not appealable under this section. Whether a particular order is a final judgment or an interlocutory order is a question that is looked at carefully in each case.

An appeal under Section 19 must be filed within thirty days from the date of the judgment or order. Missing the time limit can put the appeal in difficulty, so a person who wishes to challenge a Family Court decision should take advice promptly. Section 19(6) requires an appeal to be heard by a Bench of two or more Judges.

What cannot be appealed?

  • Section 19(2) provides that no appeal lies from a decree or order passed by the Family Court with the consent of the parties. A person who says that consent was not freely given has a different problem, and the remedy available is a matter for legal advice on the facts.
  • Section 19(2) also excludes orders under Chapter IX of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which dealt with maintenance. Section 19(4) allows the High Court to examine the record of such an order in revision. Maintenance is now dealt with in Section 144 BNSS (earlier Section 125 CrPC), and how the Act’s references operate for it is a point confirmed on the current law.
  • Apart from these provisions, Section 19(5) says that no appeal or revision lies to any court from a Family Court judgment, order or decree.

Which family matters can lead to an appeal?

The Family Courts deal with divorce and other matrimonial petitions, maintenance, custody and guardianship, restitution of conjugal rights and related matters. Any of these can end in a final judgment or order from which an appeal may be considered, subject to the points above. Orders on interim maintenance or interim custody are often interlocutory, and whether they can be challenged, and how, depends on the order and the law.

Does a family case start in the High Court?

No. Divorce, maintenance, custody and similar petitions are filed in the Family Court that has jurisdiction, or the court that the law names for the place. The High Court hears the appeal or the related proceeding afterwards. Which Family Court has jurisdiction depends on the law and the facts. See the Chennai Courts Guide and the George Town and Parrys Courts Guide. A locality name alone does not decide the court.

What does an appeal involve?

An appeal is not a fresh trial. It is heard on the record of the Family Court, so the pleadings, the evidence and the judgment are central, and the grounds of appeal must point to what the appellant says was wrong in fact or in law. The High Court may call for further material only as the law allows. The other side is given notice and can defend the judgment.

How to request a consultation

Bring the Family Court judgment or order, with the date you received it, the case number and the pleadings if you have them. The date matters because of the thirty-day limit. We will tell you at the first meeting what the options appear to be. Consultations are by appointment at West Mambalam.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • Certified or true copy of the judgment, decree or order, and the date it was received
  • Petition, written statement and the main evidence in the Family Court
  • Any interim orders, mediation or settlement records
  • Case number and the name of the Family Court
  • Marriage certificate and children’s details, where relevant
  • Papers showing any compliance steps already taken

General procedure

  1. 1Consultation, with the judgment, its date and the Family Court record.
  2. 2Checking whether the order is appealable and whether it passed with consent.
  3. 3Working out the time limit and preparing the grounds of appeal.
  4. 4Filing the appeal, with the required copies and documents, within time.
  5. 5Notice to the other side, hearing before the Bench, and judgment.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Can I go to the Madras High Court directly for a divorce or maintenance case?
No. These petitions are filed in the Family Court that has jurisdiction. The High Court hears appeals and related proceedings afterwards.
How long do I have to appeal a Family Court judgment?
Section 19(3) of the Family Courts Act, 1984 provides for an appeal within thirty days of the judgment or order. Take advice promptly, because the time can run from the date of the order.
Can an interim order of a Family Court be appealed?
Section 19(1) excludes interlocutory orders. Whether an order is interlocutory is examined in each case, so bring the order and its date to the consultation.
Can I appeal a decree that was passed by consent?
Section 19(2) says no appeal lies from a decree or order passed with the consent of the parties. What can be done if consent is said to have been improperly obtained is a question for advice on the facts.
Who hears a Family Court appeal in the High Court?
Section 19(6) requires an appeal to be heard by a Bench of two or more Judges.
Can the firm promise that an appeal will succeed?
No. The High Court decides each appeal on the record and the law, and no lawyer can promise a result.

Matrimonial & Family Law

Divorce and Matrimonial Appeals before the Madras High Court

Where a divorce decree, or the refusal of one, can be challenged, why a mutual-consent decree is treated differently, and what to check first.

Appeals against divorce and matrimonial decrees

  1. Home
  2. /
  3. Practice areas
  4. /
  5. Matrimonial & Family Law
  6. /
  7. Divorce Appeal Lawyer Madras High Court

Legal framework and scope

A divorce petition is not filed in the Madras High Court. It is filed in the Family Court, or the court the law names for the place, and the High Court comes in only afterwards, when a decree or order is challenged. This page is about that second stage. The High Court’s formal name is the High Court of Judicature at Madras, and people also search for it as the Chennai High Court. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai, and consultations are by appointment. It has no office at the High Court, George Town or Parrys Corner.

If you are looking for the divorce petition itself, see Mutual Divorce Lawyer in Chennai and Contested Divorce Lawyer in Chennai. For the general rules on appeals from all Family Court decisions, see Family Court Appeal Lawyer. Whether the firm can take up a particular appeal is confirmed at the consultation.

Can a divorce decree be appealed to the Madras High Court?

Often it can, subject to the limits in the law. A decree or final order of a Family Court in a divorce case is a judgment from which an appeal can be considered under Section 19(1) of the Family Courts Act, 1984, within thirty days under Section 19(3). The appeal may be brought by the spouse against whom a decree of divorce was passed, or by the spouse whose petition was dismissed, depending on who is aggrieved. Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 deals with appeals from decrees under that Act and is read with the Family Courts Act where a Family Court passed the decree.

The law that governs the marriage matters. Hindu marriages are under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Marriages under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 and the personal laws of other communities have their own provisions. The first step is to identify the law under which the decree was passed.

What about a mutual consent divorce decree?

A mutual consent divorce is granted on a joint petition, for Hindus under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act. Section 19(2) of the Family Courts Act says that no appeal lies from a decree or order passed with the consent of the parties. A decree granted on a joint petition is therefore generally difficult to challenge by appeal. This page does not say that every mutual consent decree is, or is not, appealable. It depends on how the decree came to be passed and on the law as the courts apply it.

A mutual consent matter can also reach a stage where no consent decree has been passed, for example where a spouse withdraws consent before the decree, or where the court has refused the petition. What remedy exists in that situation is a question for advice on the order and the record.

Which matrimonial decisions are commonly challenged?

  • A decree of divorce granted in a contested petition, challenged by the spouse who opposed it.
  • The dismissal of a divorce petition, challenged by the spouse who brought it.
  • A decree or refusal of restitution of conjugal rights, or an order on judicial separation or nullity of marriage.
  • Final orders on permanent alimony and maintenance that form part of the decree.
  • A decision on the custody or guardianship of children, where it is a final order, as dealt with on the Family Court appeal page.

What should be checked before filing a divorce appeal?

  • The date of the decree and the thirty-day limit under Section 19(3).
  • Whether the decree or order was passed with consent.
  • Whether the order is a final judgment or an interlocutory order.
  • Whether the decree has been acted on, for example by a remarriage, and what that means for the appeal. This is a question of law on the facts.
  • The grounds: what the Family Court is said to have got wrong on the evidence or on the law.

How does this differ from a Family Court appeal in general?

The general Family Court appeal page covers every kind of family order: maintenance, custody, guardianship and others. This page is limited to divorce and matrimonial decrees, where the grounds of divorce, the consent exception and the effect of the decree on the status of the parties raise their own questions.

How to request a consultation

Bring the decree or judgment, the date you received it, the petition and the written statement. Time is limited by law, so please do not wait. Consultations are by appointment at West Mambalam, and no result can be promised.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • The decree and judgment, with the date of receipt
  • The divorce petition and the written statement
  • Evidence recorded and exhibits marked in the Family Court
  • Any consent terms, settlement or mediation record
  • Marriage certificate and details of any children
  • Any later steps taken after the decree, with dates

General procedure

  1. 1Consultation, with the decree, its date and the Family Court record.
  2. 2Identifying the governing law and whether the decree passed with consent.
  3. 3Calculating the time limit and settling the grounds of appeal.
  4. 4Filing the appeal within time and notice to the other spouse.
  5. 5Hearing before the Bench, and judgment.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Can I file for divorce directly in the Madras High Court?
No. Divorce petitions are filed in the Family Court that has jurisdiction. The High Court hears appeals and related proceedings after a decision.
Can a mutual consent divorce decree be appealed?
Section 19(2) of the Family Courts Act says no appeal lies from a decree or order passed with the consent of the parties, so it is generally difficult. Whether any remedy exists depends on how the decree was passed.
What is the time limit for a divorce appeal?
Section 19(3) of the Family Courts Act provides for an appeal within thirty days of the judgment or order.
Can the spouse whose divorce petition was dismissed appeal?
A final order dismissing a petition is a judgment from which an appeal can be considered under Section 19(1). The grounds and the time limit are checked in each case.
Is a Family Court appeal the same as a divorce appeal?
A divorce appeal is one kind of Family Court appeal. The general page covers all family orders. This page covers divorce and matrimonial decrees.
Can a result be guaranteed?
No. The High Court decides each appeal on the record and the law, and no lawyer can promise a result.

Legal framework and scope

Most civil disputes are not filed in the High Court. A suit for property, a contract claim or a recovery of money is usually filed in the civil court that has jurisdiction, and the High Court comes in later, on appeal or revision. This page explains when a civil matter reaches the Madras High Court and in what capacity. The formal name is the High Court of Judicature at Madras, and it is also searched for as the Chennai High Court. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai, and consultations are by appointment. It has no office at the High Court, George Town or Parrys Corner.

For work at the trial stage, see Civil Litigation Lawyer in Chennai and Money Recovery Advocate in Chennai. For business disputes, see Corporate and Commercial Lawyer at the Madras High Court. Whether the firm can take up a particular High Court matter is confirmed at the consultation. No result can be promised.

In what capacity does the Madras High Court hear civil matters?

  • Original jurisdiction. Some suits are filed directly in the High Court, on its Original Side, depending on the subject matter and the value of the claim. This is the exception and not the rule, and it does not mean that every civil suit can be filed in the High Court.
  • Appellate jurisdiction. The High Court hears appeals against decrees and orders of lower courts, as the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and other laws provide. A first appeal against a decree is under Section 96 of the Code, and a second appeal lies only on a substantial question of law under Section 100.
  • Revisional and supervisory jurisdiction. The High Court can examine certain orders of subordinate courts in revision, for example under Section 115 of the Code, and it has a supervisory power over them under Article 227 of the Constitution.
  • Writ jurisdiction. Under Article 226 of the Constitution the High Court issues writs against the State and other authorities for the enforcement of rights. A writ petition is a different remedy from a civil suit or a civil appeal.

Does every civil suit go to the High Court?

No. A civil suit is filed in the court that has jurisdiction by subject matter, by value and by territory, and for most suits that is a civil court below the High Court. Business disputes of a specified value may go to a Commercial Court, and family matters go to the Family Court. A civil matter reaches the High Court only if it falls within one of the capacities above.

How is a civil appeal different from a revision?

An appeal is a statutory right to have the decision of a lower court re-examined on the record, on the grounds the law allows. A first appeal can examine questions of fact and law. A second appeal is confined to a substantial question of law.

A revision is narrower. It tests whether the lower court acted within its jurisdiction and followed the law in the way it decided, and it is not a re-hearing of the whole case. Whether a particular order can be appealed or only revised depends on the order and the law, and this is the first point checked.

What about time limits?

Appeals and revisions must be filed within the time prescribed by law, which varies with the kind of proceeding and is set mainly by the Limitation Act, 1963 and by special statutes. The period usually runs from the date of the decree or order. A delay can sometimes be explained to the court, but it should not be assumed that it will be condoned, so bring the order and its date to the first meeting.

Which writ matters does this page cover?

This page explains the writ jurisdiction only so that you can tell it apart from civil appeals and revisions. It does not list particular kinds of writ practice. If your question is about an order of a government body or other authority, the first step is to check whether a writ, an appeal under a special statute or a civil remedy is the right route, and whether the firm can take it up. That is confirmed at the consultation.

How to request a consultation

Bring the decree or order, the date you received it, the plaint and the written statement, or the impugned order in a writ matter, and the case number. We will tell you what the available routes appear to be. Consultations are by appointment at West Mambalam.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • The judgment, decree or order challenged, with its date
  • Plaint, written statement and issues framed
  • Evidence recorded and exhibits marked
  • Title documents, contracts or other papers on which the case turns
  • Earlier orders, interim applications and proof of compliance
  • In a writ matter, the order or action challenged and any representation made

General procedure

  1. 1Consultation, with the order, its date and the lower-court record.
  2. 2Deciding the route: appeal, revision, writ or another remedy.
  3. 3Checking the time limit and preparing the grounds.
  4. 4Filing in the High Court, with the required copies and any interim application.
  5. 5Notice to the other side, hearing and judgment.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Can I file a civil suit directly in the Madras High Court?
Only if the suit falls within the High Court’s original jurisdiction, which depends on the subject matter and the value. Most civil suits are filed in the civil courts below.
What is a second appeal?
A second appeal to the High Court under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure lies only on a substantial question of law.
What is the difference between an appeal and a revision?
An appeal is a statutory remedy that re-examines the decision on the record. A revision is narrower and tests the lower court’s jurisdiction and the way it applied the law.
Is a writ petition a civil appeal?
No. A writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is a separate remedy, usually against the State or another authority.
Does the firm have an office at the Madras High Court?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai, and consultations are by appointment.
Can the firm guarantee the outcome of an appeal?
No. The High Court decides each matter on the record and the law, and no lawyer can promise a result.

Corporate & Commercial Law

Corporate and Commercial Disputes before the Madras High Court

When a business dispute can come before the Madras High Court, which proceedings belong to other forums, and what the firm’s pages do and do not cover.

Commercial and arbitration matters before the Madras High Court

  1. Home
  2. /
  3. Practice areas
  4. /
  5. Corporate & Commercial Law
  6. /
  7. Corporate Commercial Lawyer Madras High Court

Legal framework and scope

A business dispute does not automatically belong in the High Court. Whether it is heard by a Commercial Court, by the Commercial Division of the Madras High Court, by an arbitral tribunal or by a tribunal such as the NCLT depends on the kind of dispute, its value and what the contract says. This page explains the High Court part of that picture. The formal name is the High Court of Judicature at Madras, and it is also searched for as the Chennai High Court. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai, and consultations are by appointment. It has no office at the High Court, George Town or Parrys Corner.

Shasti Law Firm’s pages describe two kinds of work in this area: commercial disputes, including before the Commercial Division of the Madras High Court, and the court applications that arise in arbitration. See Commercial Dispute Lawyer in Chennai and Arbitration Lawyer in Chennai. Whether the firm can take up a particular matter is confirmed at the consultation. No result can be promised.

Which commercial disputes can reach the Madras High Court?

Commercial disputes of a specified value are dealt with under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. Depending on the value and the territorial limits that apply, a commercial suit may be filed before a Commercial Court or, where the High Court has ordinary original civil jurisdiction, before its Commercial Division. In Chennai that means the Original Side of the Madras High Court, and the court for a particular suit is confirmed on its value and subject before filing. Appeals from commercial decisions are provided for in the Act and go to the court it names.

A commercial suit generally has to be preceded by pre-institution mediation under Section 12A of the Act, unless urgent interim relief is sought. See the commercial dispute page for the general outline.

What is the High Court’s role in arbitration?

Arbitration is a private forum chosen by agreement under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, so the contract’s arbitration clause is the first thing to read. The court comes in at particular points: interim relief under Section 9, the appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11 where the parties cannot agree, a challenge to an award under Section 34 and enforcement under Section 36. For a domestic arbitration, which court is competent for a given application depends on the Act’s definition of the court and, in some cases, on the nature of the arbitration. The firm’s page records that applications for the appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11 are made to the Madras High Court. The forum for each of the other applications is confirmed for the matter before filing.

Which proceedings belong to other forums?

  • Ordinary commercial claims below the specified value, or outside the Commercial Courts Act, go to the civil courts that have jurisdiction. See Civil Litigation Lawyer in Chennai.
  • Claims by micro and small enterprises for delayed payment may lie before the MSME Facilitation Council.
  • Cheque dishonour is a criminal complaint before a Magistrate. See Cheque Bounce Advocate in Chennai.
  • Company-law, insolvency and shareholder matters are heard by tribunals such as the NCLT and by other courts. This page does not describe them and does not say that the firm handles them.

What does the firm not claim on this page?

The firm’s pages do not list company-law proceedings, insolvency and bankruptcy work, NCLT practice, shareholder or oppression disputes, or regulatory matters. If your problem is of that kind, you are welcome to ask, but this page makes no claim that the firm acts in it, and any such matter would be confirmed with the advocate first.

How to request a consultation

Bring the contract, any arbitration clause, the notices exchanged, the amount in dispute and any order already passed. The forum is decided on those documents. Consultations are by appointment at West Mambalam.

Documents that may be needed

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • The contract, purchase orders or partnership deed
  • The arbitration clause and any notice invoking it
  • Notices, replies and correspondence on breach or default
  • Invoices, ledgers and statements of account
  • Mediation failure report under Section 12A, if one was obtained
  • Any order, award or pending proceeding on the same dispute

General procedure

  1. 1Consultation, and review of the contract and the amount in dispute.
  2. 2Deciding the forum: Commercial Court, Commercial Division, arbitration or another.
  3. 3Pre-institution mediation, where the Act requires it.
  4. 4Filing the suit or application, with the documents relied on.
  5. 5Case management, hearings and judgment, then execution or appeal.

This is a general outline. The exact steps, forum and timing vary from case to case.

Frequently asked questions

Do all commercial disputes go to the Madras High Court?
No. They go to the court or forum that has jurisdiction by value, subject and the contract. Only some commercial suits are heard by the Commercial Division of the High Court.
Can the Madras High Court appoint an arbitrator?
The firm’s arbitration page records that applications for the appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 are made to the Madras High Court where the parties cannot agree.
Is pre-institution mediation compulsory for commercial suits?
Under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 it is generally required, unless the suit contemplates urgent interim relief.
Does the firm handle NCLT or insolvency matters?
This page makes no such claim. The firm’s pages cover commercial disputes and arbitration court applications.
Does the firm have an office at the Madras High Court?
No. The firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai, and consultations are by appointment.
Can the outcome of a commercial dispute be guaranteed?
No. Courts and tribunals decide each matter on its facts and the law, and no lawyer can promise a result.

Chennai Courts Guide

Which courts sit in which district, what each kind of court generally handles and why the case decides the venue.

  1. Home
  2. /

Part 1

Official court-directory information

Taken from official court documents and pages reviewed on 8 November 2026. Listings change, so check the current official directory. This page gives no address, map or directions.

Chennai City Courts (Chennai district)

  • Principal District Court, Chennai, with Additional District Courts, including courts labelled as sitting at Singaravelar Maligai.
  • City Civil Courts and Assistant City Civil Courts, Chennai.
  • Principal Family Court, Chennai, with Additional Family Courts.
  • Court of Small Causes, Chennai.
  • Metropolitan Magistrate courts listed at Egmore (including courts at the Allikulam Complex), Saidapet and George Town.
  • Commercial Court, Egmore.
  • Special courts, such as courts for NDPS Act cases, POCSO Act cases and cases involving Members of Parliament and Legislative Assembly.

Chengalpattu District Judiciary (a separate district)

  • Combined Court Complex, Alandur: Sub Court, District Munsifs and Judicial Magistrate courts.
  • Combined Court Complex, Tambaram: Sub Court, District Munsif and Judicial Magistrate courts.
  • Single Court Complex, Pallavaram: a District Munsif-cum-Judicial Magistrate court.
  • Combined Court Complex, Chengalpattu, which is the seat of the Principal District Court for the Chengalpattu district.

Official sources: Chennai City Courts · Chennai City Courts: court directory · Chengalpattu District Judiciary · Chengalpattu: court directory · Madras High Court

Part 2

General informational guidance

Chennai and the areas around it are served by more than one district judiciary. The Chennai City Courts belong to Chennai district. Alandur, Tambaram and Pallavaram lie in the Chengalpattu district, whose judiciary was constituted separately in March 2024 when the Kancheepuram district judiciary was divided. They are not Chennai City Courts, even though they serve parts of the Chennai metropolitan area.

A court in a particular locality does not hear every kind of case from the neighbourhood. Courts are created for particular kinds of cases and for defined territories, and the assignment of a case follows from the law and from the court’s jurisdiction notifications.

Listings change. Courts are reorganised, new courts are added and cases are transferred, so the numbers and names of courts should be checked against the official directory at the time of your visit.

What kinds of matters these courts generally handle
Kind of matterGeneral position
Anticipatory bailCourt of Session or High Court; not usually a Magistrate court. See our anticipatory bail page.
Regular bail, criminal trialsMagistrate or Sessions courts, depending on the offence and stage.
Section 138 NI Act complaintsMagistrate courts. The venue turns on where the payee’s bank branch is, not on the lawyer’s location.
Divorce, custody, maintenanceFamily Courts for the district concerned, subject to territorial jurisdiction.
Civil suits and recoveryCivil courts in the relevant district, according to value and territorial jurisdiction.
Commercial disputesCommercial Courts or the High Court, depending on value and subject.
Quashing, appeals, revisionsMadras High Court.

Part 3

Case-specific jurisdiction and venue

Whether a court can hear your case depends on the subject matter, the value of the claim, the place where the cause of action arose or where the parties live or work, and any special statute that applies. For a cheque dishonour complaint, for example, the territorial rules in Section 142(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act look to the payee’s bank branch. A matter that is physically close to one court may belong to another.

A court guide such as this one cannot tell you where your own case will be heard. That is decided from the documents of the case.

Part 4What this guide does not state

This guide does not state the following. They depend on the case or on current court records, so check them with the court or your advocate.

  • Current physical address, building and floor of each court, which this guide does not state.
  • Current location of the Principal Family Court, Chennai, the City Civil Courts and the Court of Small Causes.
  • Which courts Shasti Law Firm appears before. This guide does not say that the firm appears before any particular court.
  • A bomb-blast Sessions Court of the Chennai district is listed as sitting “at Ponnamallee”. This is a special court and the guide does not treat it as a general Poonamallee court.

Listed for Saidapet in official Chennai court documents

  • Several numbered Metropolitan Magistrate courts are listed with Saidapet as their location.

Official sources: Chennai City Courts · Chennai City Courts: court directory

Part 2

General informational guidance

Metropolitan Magistrate courts are criminal courts of first instance in Chennai. They deal with complaints and police cases for offences triable by a Magistrate, and with matters such as remand and bail within their powers. The courts are organised by area, so the Saidapet courts are one of several groups of Metropolitan Magistrate courts in the city, alongside those at Egmore and George Town.

People commonly search for a “Saidapet court” in connection with cheque bounce cases because an NI Act fast-track court is listed there. That listing tells you the court exists. It does not mean every cheque case in Chennai is heard there.

Anticipatory bail is a separate matter. It is a remedy before the Court of Session or the High Court under Section 482 BNSS, and it is not usually heard by a Magistrate court at Saidapet. See our page on anticipatory bail for the forum and process.

What kinds of matters these courts generally handle
Kind of matterGeneral position
Criminal complaints before a MagistrateMetropolitan Magistrate courts try offences within their jurisdiction.
Section 138 NI Act (cheque dishonour)Handled by Magistrate courts. A dedicated NI Act fast-track court is listed at Saidapet.
Anticipatory bailNot a Magistrate-court remedy. It is heard by the Court of Session or the High Court.

Part 3

Case-specific jurisdiction and venue

The Magistrate court that hears a case depends on where the offence is alleged to have happened and on the court’s jurisdiction. For a cheque dishonour complaint, Section 142(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act ties territorial jurisdiction to the payee’s bank branch where the cheque was delivered for collection. The location of a lawyer’s office or of either party’s home does not decide this.

Jurisdiction of the individual Saidapet courts is allotted by official orders that change from time to time. This page does not set out which police stations or areas fall within them.

Part 1

Official court-directory information

Taken from official court documents and pages reviewed on 8 November 2026. Listings change, so check the current official directory. This page gives no address, map or directions.

Listed for Alandur by the Chengalpattu District Judiciary

  • Combined Court Complex, Alandur.
  • A Subordinate Judge’s court (Sub Court) and Principal and Additional District Munsif courts.
  • Judicial Magistrate Courts No. I and No. II.
  • A Judicial Magistrate, Additional Mahila Court, for criminal cases involving crimes against women.
  • A Judicial Magistrate Fast Track Court at Magisterial Level for criminal cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

Official sources: Chengalpattu District Judiciary · Chengalpattu: court directory

Part 2

General informational guidance

Alandur is in the Chengalpattu district, and its court complex is part of the Chengalpattu District Judiciary. That district was formed in 2019, and its judiciary was constituted in March 2024. People who live or work in Chennai may nevertheless find that a civil or criminal matter belongs to Alandur and not to the Chennai City Courts, so the district needs to be identified early.

The complex is described as a Combined Court Complex, meaning that civil and criminal courts of different levels are housed together. A District Munsif generally hears smaller civil claims, and a Sub Court hears claims of higher value, subject to the limits fixed by law.

Because the jurisdiction of the Magistrate courts is defined by police station areas, the investigating police station usually points to the Magistrate court that will deal with a criminal case.
