Part 1

Official court-directory information

Taken from official court documents and pages reviewed on 8 November 2026. Listings change, so check the current official directory. This page gives no address, map or directions.

Chengalpattu court complex (listed in the district directory)

  • Principal District Court and Additional District Court.
  • Family Court.
  • Mahila Court and Additional Mahila Court.
  • Commercial Courts.
  • Chief Judicial Magistrate and Judicial Magistrate Courts No. I and No. II.
  • Sub Courts and a District Munsif court.
  • A separate POCSO Court complex is also listed at Chengalpattu.

Other complexes listed for the district

  • Alandur: Subordinate Court, two Munsif courts, Judicial Magistrate Courts No. I and No. II, an Additional Mahila Court, a Customs Court and a Fast Track Court. See the Alandur Courts Guide.
  • Tambaram: Subordinate Court, a Munsif court and Judicial Magistrate Courts No. I and No. II. See the Tambaram Courts Guide.
  • Madurantakam: Subordinate Court, a Munsif court and Judicial Magistrate Courts No. I and No. II.
  • Single-court complexes at Thiruporur, Sholinganallur, Pallavaram, Thirukkalukundram and Cheyyur (the last a District Munsif-cum-Judicial Magistrate court).

Official sources: Chengalpattu District Judiciary · Chengalpattu: court directory · Madras High Court

Part 2

General informational guidance

Chengalpattu is a district of its own. Its judiciary was constituted in March 2024 when the Kancheepuram district judiciary was divided, and its district headquarters court sits at Chengalpattu. Tambaram, Alandur and Pallavaram, which many people think of as part of Chennai, fall in this district and not in the Chennai City Courts.

The district directory groups courts by complex. Chengalpattu has the fullest set, including the Principal District Court, a Family Court and Commercial Courts. Alandur, Tambaram and Madurantakam are listed as combined complexes of civil and Magistrate courts, and several smaller places have a single court. A court being listed in a place does not mean it hears every kind of case from that area.

The district page does not describe each court’s separate powers, so this guide does not either. Which court within the district takes up a particular application, including an application for anticipatory bail, is confirmed from the court’s own records for your case.

What kinds of matters these courts generally handle
Kind of matterGeneral position
Anticipatory bailCourt of Session or the Madras High Court. A Magistrate court does not usually hear it. See our anticipatory bail pages.
Regular bail and criminal trialsMagistrate courts or the Court of Session, depending on the offence and the stage.
Divorce, custody, maintenanceA Family Court, subject to territorial jurisdiction. The district directory lists a Family Court at Chengalpattu.
Civil suits and recoveryMunsif, Sub and District courts, according to value and territorial jurisdiction.
Quashing, appeals, revisionsMadras High Court.

Part 3

Case-specific jurisdiction and venue

Whether a court can hear a case depends on the subject, the stage, the value of a civil claim, and where the offence or the cause of action arose or the parties live. A police station or a postal address is a pointer, not the answer.

Tiruvallur, Kancheepuram and other neighbouring districts have their own judiciaries. This guide covers only what the Chengalpattu district directory lists.

Part 4What this guide does not state

This guide does not state the following. They depend on the case or on current court records, so check them with the court or your advocate.

  • Current address and building of each complex, which this guide does not state.
  • Which Chengalpattu court takes up an application for anticipatory bail or regular bail in a particular case.
  • Which Family Court serves a petition from a given address in the Alandur, Tambaram or Pallavaram areas.
  • Whether Shasti Law Firm appears before these courts. Nothing here says that it does, and the firm’s only office is at West Mambalam, Chennai.

Which matters does the Matrimonial & Family Law practice cover?

What does a family court lawyer do?
A family court lawyer advises on the available proceedings, prepares the petition or reply, files interim applications, appears at hearings including mediation, and represents the client through evidence and arguments. About our Criminal Law practice

A notice, a summons, an FIR or an arrest each calls for a different step, so the first task in any criminal matter is to understand exactly where it stands and which dates are running.

The services below separate protection before arrest, bail after arrest, defence at trial and petitions before the High Court. Each page sets out the framework, the documents usually needed and the general procedure.

Which code applies?Since 1 July 2024 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) have replaced the CrPC, IPC and Indian Evidence Act for new proceedings. Matters already pending, or FIRs registered before that date, may continue under the older codes, so we confirm which code applies at the first consultation.

How we approach these matters

  • Understand the stage

    We first establish whether the matter is at the notice, FIR, arrest, bail, trial or appeal stage, and what dates are pending.

  • Read the record

    The FIR, notices, remand or bail orders and any earlier court papers are reviewed before options are discussed.

  • Options and risks, plainly

    The remedies available, the forum, the risks and the likely next steps are explained in plain language.

  • No promises

    Bail and trial outcomes depend on the facts and the court’s discretion. We do not guarantee results.

Documents commonly asked for

Requirements depend on the facts of your matter; we confirm the list at the consultation.

  • Copy of the FIR or complaint, if registered and accessible
  • Any police notice or summons, including a notice under Section 35 BNSS (earlier Section 41A CrPC)
  • Government photo ID (Aadhaar, passport or voter ID)
  • Documents bearing on the allegations (agreements, receipts, messages, emails)
  • Any other records identified at the confidential consultation
  • Arrest memo and remand application
  • Certified copies of the FIR, witness statements (Section 180 BNSS, earlier Section 161 CrPC) and charge sheet
  • Medical records or seizure memos, where relevant

Frequently asked questions

Which matters does the Criminal Law practice cover?
This group covers Anticipatory Bail Advocate in Chennai, Criminal Defence Lawyer Chennai, Regular Bail Lawyer Chennai and High Court Criminal Lawyer Chennai. Each has its own page with the legal framework, documents and general procedure.
What should I bring to a first consultation?
It depends on the matter, and the list is confirmed at the consultation. Commonly asked for: copy of the FIR or complaint, if registered and accessible, any police notice or summons, including a notice under Section 35 BNSS (earlier Section 41A CrPC), government photo ID (Aadhaar, passport or voter ID) and documents bearing on the allegations (agreements, receipts, messages, emails). Please keep the first message short and leave out sensitive details.
Can anticipatory bail be sought before an FIR is registered?
It can be sought when there is a real and specific apprehension of arrest, for example after a police complaint or a notice from the investigating officer. A vague or general fear is usually not enough. Read the Anticipatory Bail Advocate in Chennai page
What is a petition under Section 528 BNSS?
It invokes the High Court’s inherent powers to quash an FIR, charge sheet or proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of court or to secure the ends of justice. It was Section 482 of the CrPC under the older law. Read the Criminal Defence Lawyer Chennai page

About our Civil Litigation & Recovery practice

Disputes over money and property turn on documents and dates: the agreement, the cheque and bank return memo, the notice sent and the reply received. This practice group covers the steps from a first legal notice through to filing and, where a decree is obtained, execution.

Cheque dishonour is an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and is pursued as a complaint before a Magistrate court, with strict statutory timelines. It is grouped here with recovery work because it usually concerns an unpaid debt, and it is set out separately below. Frequently asked questions

Which matters does the Civil Litigation & Recovery practice cover?
This group covers Legal Notice Advocate in Chennai, Money Recovery Advocate Chennai, Civil Litigation Lawyer Chennai, Cheque Bounce Advocate in Chennai and Section 138 NI Act Lawyer Chennai. Each has its own page with the legal framework, documents and general procedure.
What should I bring to a first consultation?
It depends on the matter, and the list is confirmed at the consultation. Commonly asked for: contracts, loan agreements, promissory notes or deeds, proof of payment or transaction, including bank records and any dishonoured cheque, relevant emails, messages or letters between the parties and the notice received, if a reply is to be drafted. Please keep the first message short and leave out sensitive details.
Do I have to reply to a legal notice?
There is usually no legal compulsion, but silence can be used against you later, so a measured reply is generally advisable. Avoid unadvised admissions. Read the Legal Notice Advocate in Chennai page
What is the limitation period for a money suit?
Generally three years from the date the cause of action arose, such as the date of default. A written acknowledgment of the debt can extend the period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Check your dates early. Read the Money Recovery Advocate Chennai page

Commercial disputes usually begin with a contract. The first questions are what the contract says about resolving disputes, what notice has been given and which time limits apply, and these shape the choice between arbitration and a commercial suit.

This practice group is deliberately focused: it covers arbitration and commercial litigation, including the pre-institution mediation step that applies to many commercial suits. The two service pages explain the framework and the general procedure.

Which matters does the Corporate & Commercial Law practice cover?
This group covers Arbitration Lawyer in Chennai and Commercial Dispute Lawyer Chennai. Each has its own page with the legal framework, documents and general procedure.
What should I bring to a first consultation?
It depends on the matter, and the list is confirmed at the consultation. Commonly asked for: contract containing the arbitration clause, notice invoking arbitration and any reply, statement of claim or defence with supporting documents and copy of the arbitral award (for challenge or enforcement). Can an arbitral award be challenged?
Only on the limited grounds in Section 34 of the Act, such as incapacity, invalid agreement, violation of natural justice, patent illegality or conflict with public policy. Read the Arbitration Lawyer in Chennai page
Is pre-institution mediation compulsory?
Yes, under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, unless the suit contemplates urgent interim relief. The Supreme Court has treated it as mandatory. Read the Commercial Dispute Lawyer Chennai page

Our philosophy

A few principles shape how every matter is handled.

  • The record comes first

    Advice should rest on documents, dates and the applicable law, not on assumptions or on how other matters are said to have ended.

  • Plain explanations

    Procedure, deadlines and risks are explained without needless jargon, so that you can decide how to proceed.

  • Honest about outcomes

    Results depend on facts, evidence and the court’s discretion. We do not guarantee them.

  • Confidential

    Communications between an advocate and client are protected by law (Section 132 BSA, earlier Section 126 of the Evidence Act), subject to its exceptions.

A client-focused approach

Legal problems usually arrive with deadlines and worry attached. The aim of the first consultation is to give you a clear picture of where you stand.

  • Urgent dates, such as hearings, notice periods and limitation, are identified first.
  • The options are explained together with what each involves and the risks.
  • You decide how to proceed, with the information you need to decide.
  • Please keep the first message short; sensitive details are shared at the consultation.

Our values

Integrity
We tell you where your position is strong and where it is not.
Clarity
You should leave a consultation knowing the options, the steps and the risks.
Care
Notices, petitions and affidavits are drafted with attention to limitation periods and court requirements.
Discretion
Your matter and your details are treated as confidential.

  4. 4

    The available remedies, forum, risks and next steps are explained. No result can be guaranteed.

  5. 5

    A Vakalatnama is signed and papers are drafted, verified and filed before the right court or forum.

General questions

What are the requirements for a mutual consent divorce in Chennai?
Under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, the spouses must have lived separately for at least one year, agree that they cannot live together, and settle terms on alimony, stridhan and child custody. A joint First Motion is filed in the Family Court, followed by a Second Motion after the waiting period, which the court may waive in appropriate cases.
When should someone apply for anticipatory bail?
When there is a genuine apprehension of arrest for a non-bailable offence, for example after learning of an FIR or receiving a police notice. The provision is Section 482 BNSS for proceedings under the new codes (earlier Section 438 CrPC).
What are the time limits in a cheque bounce case?
The demand notice must be sent within 30 days of the bank’s return memo. The drawer then has 15 days to pay. If unpaid, the complaint must be filed within one month after that period. Missing a step can end the remedy, so seek advice early.
Where is the office and how do I book a consultation?
The office is in West Mambalam, Chennai. Consultations are by prior appointment so that your matter can be given proper attention. Call +91 98844 41211, message on WhatsApp, or use the form on this page.

From first call to filing in five steps

What to expect

  • Documents first

    Each consultation starts with the facts and documents, so advice rests on the record and not on assumptions.

    Procedure, deadlines and risks under the BNSS, Hindu Marriage Act, NI Act and other laws are explained without needless jargon.

  • Confidentiality

    Communications between an advocate and client are protected by law (Section 132 BSA, earlier Section 126 of the Evidence Act), subject to its exceptions.

  • Careful drafting

    Petitions, notices, affidavits and pleadings are prepared with attention to limitation periods and court requirements.

  • No promises

    Outcomes depend on facts, evidence and the court’s discretion. We do not guarantee results.

Mutual Divorce · 5 min read

Mutual Consent Divorce under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act

By Shasti Law Firm, Chennai · Updated 2026-11-08

Mutual consent divorce allows spouses who agree that the marriage cannot continue to end it jointly. Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 sets out the requirements; Section 28 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 is the parallel provision for marriages registered under that Act.

What the law requires

  • The spouses have lived separately for at least one year before the petition is presented.
  • They have not been able to live together and have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved.
  • Related matters such as maintenance or alimony, stridhan, property and the custody of children are settled by agreement.

The two motions

A joint First Motion petition is filed before the Family Court. Under Section 13B(2) the Second Motion can be moved after six months and within eighteen months of the First Motion, if neither party has withdrawn consent. The court then satisfies itself and may grant the decree.

Waiving the six-month period

In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017), the Supreme Court held that the six-month period is directory, not mandatory. A Family Court may waive it where the statutory separation period has already run, reconciliation efforts have failed and waiting longer would only prolong the parties’ suffering. The court decides each case on its facts.

First year of marriage

Section 14 of the Act generally bars a divorce petition within one year of marriage unless the court grants leave on grounds of exceptional hardship or exceptional depravity.

Criminal Law · 6 min read

Anticipatory Bail under Section 482 BNSS (earlier Section 438 CrPC)

By Shasti Law Firm, Chennai · Updated 2026-11-08

The right to personal liberty is protected by Article 21 of the Constitution. Anticipatory bail lets a person who fears arrest for a non-bailable offence ask the Court of Session or the High Court in advance for a direction to be released on bail if arrested. It was provided by Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; for proceedings under the new codes the provision is Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

Which code applies

The BNSS applies to proceedings under the new codes from 1 July 2024. Matters where the FIR was registered before that date may continue under the CrPC. Which provision to cite depends on the facts, so it should be checked in each case.

What courts consider

  • The nature and gravity of the accusation.
  • The applicant’s antecedents, including any earlier convictions.
  • The possibility of the applicant fleeing from justice or tampering with evidence.
  • Whether the accusation appears to have been made to injure or humiliate the applicant.
  • Whether custodial interrogation is genuinely required.

Duration of protection

In Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020) a Constitution Bench held that anticipatory bail is not, as a rule, restricted to a fixed period, although courts may limit it where the case calls for it.

Notices from the police

A police notice requiring attendance, earlier under Section 41A CrPC and now Section 35 BNSS, is a common trigger for considering this remedy. Receiving such a notice does not itself mean arrest, but it is sensible to take legal advice before attending.

Cheque Bounce · 4 min read

Notice Timelines and Complaint Limits under Section 138 NI Act

By Shasti Law Firm, Chennai · Updated 2026-11-08

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds, or because it exceeds the arrangement with the bank, an offence if the statutory steps are followed. The timeline is strict.

The timeline

  • Present the cheque to the bank within its validity period (three months from the date on it).
  • Receive the bank’s return memo showing dishonour.
  • Send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving the memo.
  • The drawer has 15 days from receipt of the notice to make the payment.
  • If payment is not made, file the complaint within one month after that 15-day period expires.

Why dates matter

A notice sent outside the 30-day window can make the complaint not maintainable. Keep the original cheque, the return memo and proof of dispatch and delivery of the notice.

Where to file

Under Section 142(2) the court with territorial jurisdiction is generally where the payee’s bank branch is located, so the place of the payee’s account should be checked before filing.

Settlement

The offence is compoundable under Section 147, and many cases end in settlement. Courts can order costs where compounding is sought late.
